item.title: The Ripple Effect of Going for It
item.description: Can you learn to captain a yacht at 62 and turn it into a world-traveling lifestyle? Absolutely! Below, Sine Maria shares a first-hand account of her family’s latest charter with Dream Yacht in the Balearic Islands. Read on for an inspiring look at courage, partnership, and what happens when you say yes to a new adventure on the water. The Ripple Effect of Going for It On breaking into worlds you weren’t born into, and what happens when you actually do the thing. By: Good Life Designed and Sine Maria If there’s one thing I’ve learned from my mom, it’s that life has so much to offer and the limit of your world is only limited by your ability to keep expanding. In the middle of the pandemic, as part of our collective pause, she and I decided to go through the whole Good Life Designed program together again. It was through that process that she decided she wanted to be closer to nature, swim more, and learn how to sail. She didn’t grow up around sailing, knew it was costly and a bit of a boys club, but always admired the access it gave those who knew how. That hobby could take you anywhere in the world. The world of sailing requires a unique blend of resources, courage, technical education, practice, and willing crew members to go along for the ride and be there while you figure things out on your first trips alone. It thrives behind heavy yacht club doors that some are born with access into – but most don’t even know exist. The dream of being certified as a sailor has an even smaller niche- attracting those who thrive on the pressure to read and respond to the chaos of the elements at sea while holding the responsibility of passengers’ lives in their hands. Now that I have experienced the reward that comes with that kind of responsibility – I see the draw. Breaking Into a World You Weren’t Born Into I tried to look into data about women certified sailors but couldn’t find any credible data because no one seems to be particularly interested in that stat – however I can tell you there aren’t many. Sailing, just due to the nature of it, the time it requires, the unease that comes with the experience, especially as you’re getting your first solo trips under your belt, is enough to send anyone right over the edge. It’s heady, it’s overwhelming, it’s complicated, it’s technical, and it feels uncertain and dangerous before you’re skilled and experienced enough to feel truly comfortable and at ease on the water. When Pernille got the ping to learn to sail, the biggest question was how, as a 62-year-old woman, was she going to do it. She tried visiting yacht clubs but as someone who wasn’t interested in the social component and was really looking for the technical skills to captain her own ship, it didn’t feel like the best place to spend her time or money. The classes and day sail opportunities to get out on the water were nice, but if she really wanted to learn everything she needed to, she needed something different. She came across Nautilus Sailing, a week-long course in the Sea of Cortez that would teach you everything you need to know about sailing and cap off the week with a test that would certify you to sail on your own anywhere in the world. My dad at the time was in the most stressful period of his career, navigating his independent school and their 400 families through Covid. Using his coveted spring break to learn to navigate another set of uncharted territories felt not quite like the vacation he needed. But he took a leap of his own and joined her anyway. They spent a week disconnected from everything to focus on learning the thing that would later give them access to the life they live now – barely imaginable to them then. Heading out on what feel like once-in-a-lifetime week long sailing experiences all over the world with friends and family. In 6 years since becoming certified, have now completed their 15th sail and have endless shared albums to show for it. They’ve sailed all over, eight times in La Paz, Mexico, once i…

item.title: St Croix Memorial Sail Moment of Zen
item.description: 🇻🇮 St. Croix St Croix Memorial Sail Moment of Zen Steve There’s sadness at the end of every sail. So too at the end of every life. When the two things come together, though, it can be beautiful. Such was the case with a July 2026 memorial sail back in St. Croix , the tail end of which is featured here. This sail celebrated the life of an old childhood friend . We sailed with his family and friends to a spot just offshore Judith’s Fancy . Ashes were scattered to the sea. A wreath, Cruzan Rum , and a few Heinekens were too. Captain Carl blew his conch shell consecrating the moment. There were tears for sure, but mostly there was love, laughs, and smiles. It was heavy, it was fun. It was meaningful, unforgettable, and deeply moving, much as any life that’s been fully and truly lived to the fullest. Last updated by Steve Bennett on 09/23/2026 . item.title: French Polynesia Cabin Cruise: The Floating Boutique Hotel for Effortless Island Hopping
item.description: Imagine waking up in a comfortable suite aboard a premium catamaran. You stretch out on crisp sheets and wonder what spectacular view is awaiting you today. Will it be the majestic twin peaks of Bora Bora or the white sand beaches and tropical jungles of Huahine? You step on deck and sniff the air: today’s port is actually the vanilla-scented shores of Taha’a. That’s what life is like aboard a French Polynesia cabin cruise. Every day, you get to go on a new adventure. At night, you rest and relax in the comfort of a spacious cabin aboard a shared catamaran charter. For many travelers, the freedom to visit multiple destinations rather than be confined to a single resort makes a cabin cruise a much better option than a typical holiday on land. What Is a French Polynesia Cabin Cruise? A French Polynesia catamaran cruise or cabin cruise is a travel option where you book a private cabin with its own attached bathroom on a catamaran. Instead of chartering an entire yacht yourself, you share the vessel with a small group of other travelers. How Cabin Cruises Work The catamaran operates much like a small-scale cruise ship but with a personalized touch. Your captain navigates the islands, and an onboard steward prepares your meals. This vacation style eliminates the stress of trip planning, sailing logistics, and meal preparation. And since vessels are shared among travelers, cabin cruises are more affordable than booking Tahiti yacht charters . Why It Feels Like a Floating Boutique Hotel Unlike massive cruise ships that carry thousands of passengers, a catamaran hosts between 8 and 12 guests. This creates an intimate atmosphere, similar to that of a small hotel, except you also get to experience different destinations and activities every day. In French Polynesia, our cabin cruises are offered on the Bali 5.4, Lagoon 620, and the Fountaine Pajot Ipanema 58, each accommodating 12 guests. Comfort and Convenience: What Is a Cabin Cruise Like Onboard? Life aboard a cabin charter is defined by relaxation and comfort. Your catamaran features decks, shaded outdoor dining areas, and a forward trampoline net. This net is a great spot to lounge as the islands glide by. No jostling for sunbathing space on crowded beaches or lining up to rent gear from stands along the shore. You can get all the sun you want on deck, and the cruise includes the use of water sports equipment. You can step directly off the yacht’s transom steps into the water, swim, snorkel, or kayak to your heart’s content. Island Hopping Without Repacking or Airport Transfers With 118 islands and atolls spread across an area as vast as Western Europe, French Polynesia island hopping is all about discovering the unique character of each destination. However, having your base camp be a hotel or resort limits your options. It also means you have to go through a drawn-out process of getting there before you can visit each different island. Traditional travelers must pack their suitcases, check out of their resorts, take a taxi to the airport, wait in security lines, and fly to the next island, only to repeat the check-in process. Meanwhile, on Tahiti cabin cruises , you unpack your bags once on arrival. While you relax on deck or sleep in your cabin, the catamaran moves you between Tahiti and other destinations like Huahine, Raiatea, Taha’a, and Bora Bora. A Tahiti cabin charter eliminates the need for regional flights and ferry schedules, saving you both travel stress and vacation time. Space, Food, Privacy, and Seasickness: Honest Answers Before booking a sailing trip, it is normal to have a few questions about how things work on a boat. Here is what daily life aboard your shared luxury catamaran looks like. Space: Yacht cabins are smaller than hotel rooms, but they’re just as well-appointed. They feature built-in storage and ensuite bathrooms, with air-conditioning at specified daylight hours when you want a break from the tropical heat. Food: Your steward handles all the grocery …

item.title: Tropical Ice Goddess: Hot New Ice Cream Shop in St Croix
item.description: 🇻🇮 St. Croix Tropical Ice Goddess: Hot New Ice Cream Shop in St Croix Steve For as long as I (and likely most every other Crucian) can remember, you had to head west to Frederiksted for the best ice cream on St. Croix . Specifically, you had to head to Armstrong’s Ice Cream . As I noted in an earlier post… …if you want to get a real taste of [St Croix], Armstrong’s is a must. On my most recent STX visit (July 2026), though, I discovered a new contender to St Croix’s ice cream throne. Her name: Tropical Ice Goddess. Seduced by Soca Siren Songs To be clear, I did not actually meet the Goddess herself. I did, however, come across her ice cream shop located in the heart of Christiansted. Despite it’s bright and cheery facade, though, I might’ve missed Tropical Ice Goddess entirely if not for the sweet soca music blaring from its front patio. Could the ice cream treats inside match the sweetness of the soca coming from the shop? I had to investigate… Inside Tropical Ice Goddess | Photo by Steve Bennett Inside, Tropical Ice bore every resemblance to your typical, run-of-the-mill ice cream shop. Big cooler filled with vats of ice cream. Various toppings, cups, and spoons spread atop the counter. Nothing altogether that uncommon. Then, I noticed the flavors. Flavors for Days All of the ice cream served at Tropical Ice Goddess is proudly homemade in St Croix. Traditional faves like chocolate, vanilla, rocky road, cookie dough, strawberry, and mint chocolate were all there. So too were more West Indian sorbet flavors like mango, guava, and soursop. Tropical Ice Goddess also carries a KitKat ice cream option and something called Red Hot Teaser, which is made from Red Hots cinnamon candies. Kinda crazy, right? (Fun fact: The most popular ice cream flavor at Tropical Ice Goddess is Fudge Peanut.) All of those flavors were enticing in their own special ways. What really caught my attention, though, was the broad array of boozy options. Boozy Sweets Honey Whiskey. Baileys Strawberry. Guavaberry Coquito. Ponche Kuba. Painkiller. Cruzan Rum Raisin. Captain Morgan Spiced Cherry Chocolate. Peanut Punch Screwball. Muttiny (Vodka) PR Coffee. Clearly, this ice cream shop isn’t just for kids! Tropical Ice Goddess Grab & Go Cocktail Menu | Photo by Steve Bennett Aside from all of the various ice cream flavors, Tropical Ice Goddess also specializes in “Grab & Go” cocktails. The homemade mamajuana alone is worth ducking in here, if you ask me. Typical bar food – pizza, burgers, hot dogs – are also on the menu. There really is something here for everyone. That includes vegans and those with gluten dietary concerns. The place is pretty great, especially with the soca jammin’ all out into the street! Better Than Armstrong’s? So, yeah, Tropical Ice Goddess is a new must-stop for me in Christiansted moving forward. At the same time, I’m not ready to crown it over Armstrong’s just yet. Not necessarily. If you love your sweet treats with a bit of booze, though, then you just might! If You Go… Tropical Ice Goddess St Croix is located at 2220 Queen Cross Street in Christiansted. (See map below.) They’re open every single day beginning at noon. Closing time is 7PM on Monday and Tuesday, 8PM on Wednesday and Sunday, 9PM on Thursday, and 10PM on Friday and Saturdays. Last updated by Steve Bennett on 08/11/2026 . Personally, though, I love the wild natural beauty of Hams Bay. 🇻🇮 St. Croix Boiler Bay, St. Croix Cottongarden Point divides Boiler Bay with Cramer Park, the beach we frequented most often during our childhood in St. Croix. item.title: Hiking the Cinnamon Bay Nature Loop, St. John
item.description: 🇻🇮 St. John Hiking the Cinnamon Bay Nature Loop, St. John Steve Few photos better exemplify a hike than this one that I snapped along the Cinnamon Bay Nature Loop in Saint John . That is to say, it’s a cute little hike. MUCH more nature stroll than arduous adventure. Soft. Cuddly. Doesn’t sound like one of our typical excursions into the wilds of the Caribbean, does it? Yeah, it’s not. Still, the Cinnamon Bay Nature Loop is worth checking out…under the right circumstances. Up in the wilds of the Cinnamon Bay Nature Loop, St. John | Photo by Steve Bennett For me and the wife, those “right circumstances” during our November 2024 STJ escape centered on the primary reason for the trip: our 25th wedding anniversary. Sure, the wife and I love hiking. In fact, she’s the one who rekindled my love for traipsing around in the bush during our June 2010 trip to Nevis . (See The Source Hiking Trail and Rekindling Romance in Nevis post for more on that dramatically more challenging adventure.) We planned our St. John escape, though, to be all about relaxing and reconnecting. Nothing too strenuous. At least not outside of our romantic hideaway, if you know what I mean. Anyway, after lunch and a dip at Cinnamon Bay , we decided to give this soft adventure a try. Almost immediately, we were happy that we did. The Nature Loop starts just across the street from the entrance to the Cinnamon Bay parking lot. In total, it stretches just .5 miles. The footing is generally great throughout, especially as a portion of the trail runs over a wooden boardwalk. Nature Loop boardwalk | Photo by Steve Bennett Helpful signage in pretty good shape is also scattered along the route, providing insights into points of interest. Nature Loop signage | Photo by Steve Bennett Among those points of interest: ruins of the old Cinnamon Bay Sugar Plantation . Sugar Factory Ruins at Cinnamon Bay, Saint John | Photo by Steve Bennett Cinnamon Bay Sugar Plantation Ruins | Photo by Steve Bennett Amidst the forest shadows and filtered sunlight, the ruins espoused a heightened poignancy, the haunted legacy hanging heavy in the air. Seconding that emotion, eerie tombs like these… Cinnamon Bay Nature Loop tombs | Photo by Steve Bennett I gotta say, I was not expecting anything like this. We encountered two different clusters of tombs along the Cinnamon Bay Nature Loop. One of the pair pictured here, the final resting spot of Margarethe Berner Hjardemaal , dates back to 1836. Any spooky feeling that we had along the Nature Loop, though, were more than tempered by cute forest companions, like the pictured at the head of this post. White-tailed deer in Cinnamon Bay, St. John | Photo by Steve Bennett We came across more than 20 white-tailed deer over our .5-mile jaunt. Friendly Cinnamon Bay deer | Photo by Steve Bennett Unlike the deer I grew up knowing in St Croix, these guys were not skittish or shy at all. In fact, they seemed quite happy and comfortable welcoming us into their world. They grazed within a few feet of us, never even hinting at being alarmed in any way as we passed through. So yeah, the Cinnamon Bay Nature Loop is very short and easy. At the same time, though, it’s full of surprises. If you’re looking for a soft yet rewarding intro to St. John hiking adventures, this is it! Last updated by Steve Bennett on 03/04/2026 . Related Posts 🇻🇮 St. John Rejoicing in Cinnamon Bay, St John: Wish You Were Here Cinnamon Bay, St. John is so beautiful that immediately upon seeing it you're compelled to raise your hands to the heavens in celebration. 🇻🇮 St. John Cinnamon Bay St John – Pure Beach Sweetness Cinnamon makes the Holiday Season sweet, but we prefer the sunny/salty seasoning of Cinnamon Bay St John for our Christmas celebrations. 🇻🇮 St. John Post-Hurricane Irma St John Healing Along Cinnamon Bay The healing inherent in this image extends beyond the usual beachy comforts. This is post-Hurricane Irma St John, the island itself, healing.

item.title: Great Pond Bay Mystery Wall, St Croix
item.description: 🇻🇮 St. Croix Great Pond Bay Mystery Wall, St Croix Steve One of the great joys I’ve derived from producing Uncommon Caribbean is noting all the many things that our islands have in common. Sometimes it’s a culinary dish or fruit that goes by a different name, depending on where you’re enjoying it. Genips , and the different varieties of fried dough – fry bake , Johnny Cakes , festivals , etc. – are prime examples. Other times it’s the shared elements among our musical traditions, popular sayings, and more. Then there’s the curious case of the Great Pond Bay mystery wall. Wall Outta Nowhere I happened upon it while hiking along Great Pond Bay on the southern coast of STX a few years ago. I had no idea what it was, or had been. At the same time, though, it looked very familiar. Great Pond Bay Mystery Wall | Photo by Steve Bennett Not like anything I’d seen elsewhere in Saint Croix, though. This mystery wall reminded me of somewhere else… Months went by, then a couple years. All the while my curiosity with the wall remained. I’d hoped to investigate it further on my next trip back home. Before I could, though, I found myself in Sint Eustatius staring at this… Statia warehouse ruins | Photo by Steve Bennett Faint Echoes of Statia Now, I’ll grant you that the ruins are decidedly different. The Great Pond Bay mystery wall is primarily comprised of jagged rocks. The rocks that make up the Statia ruins, though, are smooth. Still, I think it’s more the location right along the sea that made the connection in my mind. The ruins in St. Eustatius, I knew, were from Dutch colonial era warehouses. They’re located along the waterfront in the main commercial area of the capital city, Oranjestad. The Great Pond Bay mystery wall, though, sits on the remote south coast of Saint Croix, far from the historically significant commercial areas in Christiansted or Frederiksted. So, what gives with this wall? Great Pond Bay Mystery Wall Mystery Solved That was a water mill that was up on top the Bluff 150 years ago. So says John Farchette, a former Park Ranger with St. Croix’s East End Marine Park . I got his take through my old STX high school friend, Roy Pemberton. According to John, the bluff in question was eroded significantly over the years by several hurricanes. The big blow, though, was delivered by Hurricane Hugo in 1989. The most infamous storm in St. Croix’s history undermined the mill’s foundation, causing the full structure to come crashing down along the shore/into the sea. So yeah, there’s some ancient colonial history in this mystery wall, though not quite along the lines of what was linking up in my mind. If you go… My “not so mysterious after all” mystery wall is easy to find. Just head to the St. Croix East End Marine Park Office , trek down to the shore, and make a right. The wall is located about a five-minute walk down the beach. Last updated by Steve Bennett on 01/23/2026 . item.title: Aruba Travel Guide
item.description: Aruba is flat (highest peak: 617 feet), generally windy, dry (avg. annual rainfall: less than 20 inches), and every bit the tourist trap most uncommon travelers think it is… but that doesn’t mean you should avoid this multi-cultural southern Caribbean gem. On the contrary, the island’s well-trod attractions and Spring Break-style party scene are confined to the island’s western regions. Specifically, the areas around Palm Beach, Eagle Beach, and the capital, Oranjestad. So, that leaves the vast majority of Aruba’s 70 square miles open and available for the type of uncommon exploration and unique experiences we love! Check out small fishing villages like Savantea, where you can enjoy the freshest seafood on the island. Journey to San Nicholas, Aruba’s “Second City” located on the southeastern shore, and stop in for a friendly drink and an introduction to Aruba’s history and gritty underbelly at Charlie’s Bar. Nearby Baby Beach is a well-kept secret among locals for offering all the natural splendor of Aruba’s more famous sandy stretches… except crowds, high-rise hotels, and glitzy casinos. The island’s north shore reveals even greater uncommon pursuits harkening back to Aruba’s Amerindian history and Gold Rush period . No matter where you go in Aruba, you’re sure to encounter some of the friendliest and most diverse people anywhere in the region. Almost everyone speaks Dutch, Spanish, English, and Papiamento, a unique Afro-Portuguese dialect that also includes some Arawak elements. It’s spoken only in Aruba, Bonaire, and Curaçao. Aruba’s melting pot of cultures is reflected in local cuisine, cultural events, native arts and crafts, music, and dance traditions. leaving much to discover beyond the party zone… Last updated by Patrick Bennett on 01/07/2026 .

item.title: St. Croix, US Virgin Islands Travel Guide
item.description: St. Croix is home. Being born and bred Crucians, the island holds an extra-special place in our hearts. Not only were our hearts and minds nurtured here, so too was our enduring love for the Caribbean; the same love that inspired us to create Uncommon Caribbean in the first place. St. Croix is, of course, much more than our collection of utopian childhood memories. Today, it’s a destination in flux. Alternating periods of booms and busts have yielded profound socio-economic changes in recent years. Many native-born Crucians, like us, have left the island to pursue opportunities overseas. At the same time, a population influx, primarily from the Continental United States, has brought new ideas, investments, cruise ships, real estate shifts, and opportunities to our home island’s shores. St. Croix is still plenty sweet, though in the process of all this change, some feel it has lost a bit of its “Caribbean melting pot” cachet. In our St. Croix travel guide, we square the old with the new, all the while highlighting our home island’s natural splendor, unique traditions, and charms to show you why this is still one of the Caribbean islands that you won’t want to miss. Watch this video on YouTube How to get to St. Croix No Passport Required St. Croix Beaches Where to Eat St. Croix Map Know Before You Go How to get to St. Croix Depending on where you’re departing from, getting to St. Croix can be reasonably simple. By Air From the continental United States, Spirit, Jetblue, Delta, and American Airlines all serve Henry E. Rohlsen International Airport (STX) with daily arrivals. The only issue is the lack of enough direct flights. Coming from the Northeast United States, you can expect a layover in Miami (MIA), Fort Lauderdale (FLL), or San Juan (SJU). If you’re starting your trip from further west, you may connect through Dallas (DFW). None of those connections are too bad. (Patrick, though, has a particular dislike for the service at MIA!) By Seaplane! Another novel (and super fun) way to arrive in style on St. Croix is via seaplane aboard Seaborne Airlines ! Even better, lining up a seaplane transfer allows you to take advantage of the many direct flights to St. Thomas! And once you get to St. Thomas, it’s just a 25-minute flight from downtown Charlotte Amalie to downtown Christiansted, St. Croix. When Steve and I were growing up, the Virgin Islands Seaplane Shuttle was an essential link from St. Croix to the rest of the world. So, it’s wonderful that today’s travelers can also experience this more unique way to travel! (By the way, if you long for the bygone era of the VI Seaplane Shuttle, check out our Virgin Islands Seaplane Shuttle t-shirt in our shop!) No Passport Required The #1 draw for many Americans traveling to St. Croix: No passport is required! Note: Just so that we’re 100% clear on this, St. Croix, the largest of the United States Virgin Islands, is a part of the United States of America (USA). The official political status of the United States Virgin Islands relative to the Federal Government of the United States of America is that of an unincorporated U.S. territory. This is just like Puerto Rico, though somewhat more so like Guam or American Samoa, at least from the standpoint of U.S. political history. (Don’t worry, we’re not going to test you on this.) St. Croix and the rest of the United States Virgin Islands (including St. John and St. Thomas) have been a part of the United States for more than 100 years—ever since the Treaty of the Danish West Indies in 1917. St. Croix Beaches The story of St. Croix is about much more than beautiful beaches . But if you think the island is lacking in this regard, you’d be wrong. In fact, one of our favorite beaches in the world graces the island. Of course, we’re totally biassed, and of course, we’re talking about Sandy Point . item.title: Hvar Island Croatia: a must-visit sailing destination?
item.description: Where can you find the sunniest beach vacation in Europe? Greece, Italy, Spain – certainly all top contenders. But ask anyone who’s sailed to Hvar Island, Croatia, and they’ll confirm the abundance of warm sunshine in this hidden Mediterranean gem…just one of many reasons to plan a visit! From secluded coves to vibrant fishing villages, artisanal vineyards to ancient castles, Hvar Island’s stunning coastlines and hidden treasures are crying out to be explored by boat. Are you ready to plan your dream Mediterranean yacht charter vacation? Here’s what makes this destination a must-see and how to make the most of your sailing adventure in Croatia’s Hvar Island. How To Plan Your Yacht Charter in Hvar Island Croatia Is a yacht charter right for me? The top benefits of sailing in Hvar Island Top things to do in Hvar How to travel to Hvar Island by yacht The best times to visit Hvar Island How to plan a sailing vacation in Croatia and Hvar How To Plan Your Yacht Charter in Hvar Island Croatia Is a Hvar Island yacht charter right for me? If you hope to spend your vacation fully immersed in the magic of the Mediterranean, you can’t stay on land. Imagine waking up to the gentle rocking of crystal-clear turquoise waters before drinking your morning coffee with panoramic ocean views. This is just a snapshot of what makes a yacht charter the ultimate way to experience this Croatian paradise! Allows for spontaneity A yacht charter allows you to explore Croatia’s islands entirely at your own pace. Unlike land-based accommodation, where you must start and end your day at the same hotel, a yacht charter allows for a flexible itinerary. This means you and your vacation crew can be spontaneous with your plans and travel from one beautiful spot to the next without having to repack your suitcase. Exclusive access to some of the best beaches A yacht charter offers exclusive access to hidden beaches and secluded coves that are inaccessible by land. While tourists crowd the main beaches, you’ll be floating in quiet, pristine bays that make you feel like the only travellers on the island. Less logistics = less stress Finally, yacht charters help reduce travel logistics. Instead of navigating crowded ferries and booking multiple hotels or transfers, your comfortable accommodation moves with you, freeing up your time to experience as much of Hvar as possible. Top things to do in Hvar Hvar has earned the nickname ‘the Croatian St. Tropez”, and for good reason. With its blend of natural beauty, rich history, and vibrant culture, the island paradise is both luxurious and relaxing, yet jam-packed with opportunities for adventure. At its heart is Hvar Town, an ancient village known for its stunning Venetian architecture, 13th-century walls, and the impressive Fortica fortress overlooking the harbor. It’s absolutely worth spending an afternoon wandering the polished limestone streets to uncover the island’s rich history. For true island hoppers, no visit would be complete without exploring the breathtaking Pakleni Islands – an archipelago just off Hvar’s southwest coast. With your Croatia Yacht Charter , you’ll have the perfect platform to sail across azure waters, dance at popular beach clubs, and hike pine-scented walking paths. For wine enthusiasts, Hvar’s sunny terrain produces some of Croatia’s finest wines. One popular tasting method is to anchor in Stari Grad and venture inland to visit family-run wineries powered by ancient winemaking techniques. The island’s signature Plavac Mali grape creates particularly robust reds! Active travellers will love hiking the island’s rugged interior, where lavender fields and ancient hamlets dot the trails. For a cool down, consider paddleboarding around your yacht’s latest bay! For night owls, there’s no shortage of nightlife excursions. item.title: The Real Caribbean Less Traveled
item.description: For years, the Caribbean has been marketed by those not native to these immaculate shores as nothing but sand, sun, and cheap rum. All good things (well, except the bad rum part), but that barely scratches the surface! We’re Steve and Patrick Bennett, West Indian brothers with a passion for Caribbean travel and culture. And we’d like to welcome you to Uncommon Caribbean , a celebration of the little covered charms of the Antilles! From the unexpected ( climbing the tallest mountain in North America east of the Rockies ) to the classic ( like the story behind the classic daiquiri ) to the historic (like Anguilla’s sailing traditions ) to the delicious (like this secret recipe shhh ) to exploring our home island of St. Croix, our mission is to take you on an engaging journey beyond the region’s well-trod sun, sand, and sea attractions to reveal a unique side of the Caribbean seldom featured in traditional travel guides. Over 150,000 fans can’t be wrong. Follow us. Watch this video on YouTube Who We Are Steve and Patrick Bennett of Uncommon Caribbean Steve Bennett Editorial Director PR guy by trade, West Indian by birth, Steve has been helping journalists tell stories about the Caribbean for the past 20+ years. As co-founder, editorial director, and principal voice of Uncommon Caribbean , Steve shares a personal and uniquely informed view of the authentic side of Caribbean travel and culture every day. Steve’s travels have taken him to 45 Caribbean destinations (and counting), many of which he’s visited while leading media tours as the head of his travel-focused public relations agency, SBPR Corp. This depth of experience has taught him that the uncommon is not relegated to the region’s most far-flung and little-known destinations. Every corner of the Caribbean has something special to offer adventurous, culturally curious travelers. The uncommon is everywhere, even in the most touristy destinations. We help you find and enjoy the best, most rewarding travel experiences that our region has to offer no matter where you may roam. Steve resides in Fort Lauderdale, FL, though his heart remains in his beloved home island of St. Croix , U.S. Virgin Islands . Patrick Bennett Creative Director With 15+ years of experience producing winning creative at top New York-based ad agencies, Patrick has earned a reputation for reinventing consumer brands. This, of course, fits hand in glove with Uncommon Caribbean’s mission to refresh how people think about Caribbean travel. It’s an ambitious task, but this born and bred Crucian has already managed similar feats for the likes of Samsung, Kraft, Six Flags, Verizon, and others; so we’re feeling pretty good about having him in charge. Did we mention he’s also got a passion for photography ? Patrick may call Brooklyn home, but you’re just as likely to find him traipsing across some distant, exotic land experiencing local cultures… Camera in hand. item.title: Soggy Dollar Bar Webcam Puts You On The Beach In The BVI’s
item.description: 🇻🇬 British Virgin Islands Soggy Dollar Bar Webcam Puts You On The Beach In The BVI’s Steve White Bay, Jost Van Dyke. Party central in the British Virgin Islands. Sun-kissed days bring scores of boaters here for one of the best beach party scenes anywhere in the Caribbean. So synonymous is White Bay with Painkiller -fueled fun that it’s hard to imagine these shores sans people on a sunny day. Thanks to COVID-19, though, the Soggy Dollar Bar Webcam is currently showing a different story. As we’ve mentioned previously, Soggy Dollar ranks among the most legendary Caribbean beach bars. As you can see, the bar’s location is a big plus. So too is the colorful backstory that spawned Soggy Dollar’s name and the overall vibe. As I wrote a few years back… …the place [Soggy Dollar Bar] has all the makings for me. A mostly outdoor setting in the sand; random flags, stickers, and patches left behind by happy patrons; strong drinks; an insanely pristine beach – what’s not to love? Actually, Patrick did find a few things he didn’t particularly love on his last visit a few years back. In all fairness, he’s not into Painkillers or the mostly sweet drink options at Soggy Dollar. Also, neither of us like our Caribbean beaches too crowded. On Patrick’s visit, White Bay smacked more Spring Break in the Florida Panhandle than the West Indies. Yeah, not ideal in our uncommon sense of beach liming… As the Soggy Dollar Bar Webcam shows, though, crowds are not a problem right now. And personally I like Painkillers. How about you..? Wanna’ join me here once the time is right to see how the Soggy Dollar legend is holding up..? item.title: Sweet Sorrow Sailing Away Aboard the Saba Rock Ferry
item.description: 🇻🇬 British Virgin Islands Sweet Sorrow Sailing Away Aboard the Saba Rock Ferry Steve I’m not typically envious of sad occurrences. The scene, a boatload of happy folks sailing away aboard the Saba Rock Ferry , elevates my feelings of envy to new heights. item.title: Antigua and Barbuda Travel Guide
item.description: Antigua often gets the most love for its fabled 365 beaches. And trust us, those strips of white sand are tremendous. We’ve even tried to visit all 365. Including Antigua’s one nude beach ! But, if beaching it is the only reason you intend to visit, you’ll miss out on a lot. The beaches are just the beginning How to get to Antigua Antigua Beaches Where to Eat Where to Stay Antigua Hurricane Season Don’t forget Barbuda The Bottom Line Antigua Map Know Before You Go The beaches are just the beginning By far the best time of year to visit is during Sailing Week . This wild annual event features well over 100 yachts from all over the world. Even some of the world’s most awe-inspiring superyachts come to race. There’s also plenty of local sailing talent on display. And besides the action on the water, you can expect parties day and night. Top musical talent from around the world comes to the island during this week to put on a show. Antigua also makes access to its rich British colonial history easy. Forts dot the landscape in some of the most picturesque locations. Nelson’s Dockyard (named for Admiral Horatio Nelson who made his base here), Fort Barrington overlooking the brilliant crescent of Deep Bay , Shirley Heights , Fort James , Fort Berkeley—they all welcome visitors to take a stroll through history. Plus there are plenty of hikes dotting the island . Everything from like hikes to scaling Mount Obama (formerly known as Boggy Peak), the highest point on Antigua. Also harkening back to the island’s sugar plantation past, are the over 100 windmills peppered throughout. And for those who want their history more concentrated, the capital city of St. John additionally has numerous historic elements sprinkled within and is worth exploring. How to get to Antigua Antigua’s all-new and state-of-the-art VC Bird International Airport (ANU) offers plenty of direct flight options on a number of airlines. Many at great prices. Which airlines fly direct to Antigua? American Airlines and JetBlue are you’re best chance for a direct flight from the United States, although Delta and United might also offer direct service depending on your departing airport. Antigua Beaches Yes, your space in the sun is world-renowned for its magnificent strips of sand bordering brilliant Eastern Caribbean seas, so we can’t completely discount spending some time enjoying the embarrassment of riches on offer. Think blazing white sand without a spec of black sand in the bunch. We’ve spent time on many of these beaches ourselves for… Umm… Research. Here are some of our favorites! Darkwood Beach Darkwood Beach Normally, my favorite beaches are the ones that are the hardest to get to. The elusive strips of sand that require a boat or a kayak or repelling down a rope ladder or at least tramping through the bush. Darkwood Beach is one exception. It’s literally by the side of the road. And it’s still stunning. Long Bay Beach Long Bay Beach Found in the extreme northeast of the island Long Bay Beach delivers the quintessential Antigua beach experience. Expect to find a small open-air restaurant where you can buy beers and rum, friendly local families bathing in the sea, almost impossibly white sand, and electric blue waters. There are also some small stands selling some fairly touristy wares, but they’re easily ignored if that’s not your thing. Galley Bay Beach While this beach is connected to a resort, it’s worth mentioning because, well, it’s connected to a resort! Guests who stay at the Galley Bay Antigua Resort can expect to wake up every morning to one of the best beaches the island has to offer. Calm cool seas, sand at the precisely perfect temperature and consistency, plus tropical sunrises that can’t be beat. Antigua Nude Beach Eden Beach, Hawksbill Bay For those looking for the most unusual beach on the island, Eden Beach is certainly a contender. Why? Because it holds the distinction of being Antigua’s only clothing-optional beach . Yes, there’s a nude beach a…

item.title: The Indians BVI – Uncommon Attraction
item.description: 🇻🇬 British Virgin Islands The Indians BVI – Uncommon Attraction Steve Tons of places and things in the Caribbean carry Amerindian names. The rocks pictured here, though, are actually called “The Indians.” They’re found in the British Virgin Islands just west of Pelican Island . As such, The Indians is a prime point of interest for the thousands of sailing enthusiasts that flock to the BVIs each year. They come as much for the uniquely uncommon beauty of the rocks as the treasures found beneath the waves here. The snorkeling and diving here are great. So great, in fact, that The Indians consistently ranks as the #2 most popular dive site in the British Virgin Islands. So, what does any of this have to do with the native peoples who originally inhabited the BVIs? Well…actually…nothing. At least as far as we can tell. Indeed, “The Indians” name assigned to these rocks refers instead to its appearance. To some, it seems, the four rocks towering a good 50 feet from the sea look like a Native American headdress . Truthfully, I’m not sure that I see it. You’ll likely have difficulty seeing it too (and enjoying undersea adventures here) if you sail over to The Indians any time besides first thing in the morning. As one of the top scuba/snorkel attractions in the BVI, this spot is often quite crowded. So yeah, you’ll definitely want to get here and get underwater as early as possible. *Photo by Patrick Bennett Last updated by Steve Bennett on 01/11/2023 . item.title: Saba Rock Returns! Legendary BVI Resort Island Sets October 2021 Reopening
item.description: 🇻🇬 British Virgin Islands Saba Rock Returns! Legendary BVI Resort Island Sets October 2021 Reopening Steve The slowly decaying ruins of previously grand hotels lay scattered throughout the Caribbean. They are, at once, sad legacies of tragic hurricanes long past, shattered dreams, and poor foresight. Thankfully, Saba Rock is not among them. At least it won’t be when it reopens, slightly bigger, more luxurious, and better than ever, in October 2021. Memories of Old Saba Rock The old Saba Rock was pretty cool. Easily among the most uncommon private island outposts in the British Virgin Islands , the one-acre resort enclave was particularly popular with scuba divers. Its founder and original owner, scuba and treasure hunting legend Bert Kilbride, was the reason why. (Editor’s note: Check out the old property in this long ago post from the UC archives.) In September 2017, though, the good times that Bert originally birthed here came to an end. Hurricane Irma was the reason why. Fast forward to today, 2021, and the new Saba Rock. 100% Rebuilt Artist rendering of the new Bar/Restaurant Well beyond the type of modest refurbishment that other resorts count as “full renovations,” the new Saba Rock has been completely rebuilt from the ground up. While the new structure is more storm-resistant, style is certainly not being sacrificed in its design and construction. Living space (artist rendering) The old SR had eight guest rooms. Now, the resort boasts a total of nine rooms and suites. Not a huge change, I know, but it’s the enhanced elegance now espoused throughout the new Saba Rock that truly separates the resort’s luxurious present from its past. Sleek, Stylish, but Still All About The Sea Artist rendering of a new guest room From these renderings, it’s clear to see that the new resort will feature a rather sleek contemporary design. Earth tones dominate, while large windows keep the resort’s most luxurious feature, its beautiful surrounding seascapes, in the spotlight. Fun and colorful design elements, like the surfboards above, further echo the sea and the myriad of fun marine activities on offer at Saba Rock. Saba Rock Grand Opening Sale Considering that we never made it to the old Saba Rock, we are seriously excited about the opening of the new version! If you are too, the resort is offering a Stay & Play Grand Opening special to entice you even further. The deal: book four nights and pay for three. The promo also includes complimentary daily breakfast, round-trip ferry transfers from Gun Creek and Leverick Bay, and a special surprise welcome gift. Stay & Play Grand Opening incentives apply to resort stays enjoyed between October 15 and November 20, 2021. Nightly rates start at US$750 based on double occupancy. For reservations and more information, be sure to check in with our friends at Saba Rock online. Last updated by Steve Bennett on 08/18/2021 . item.title: At The Baths in The BVI’s, One Month After Irma
item.description: 🇻🇬 British Virgin Islands At The Baths in The BVI’s, One Month After Irma Steve One month. For most of us, it doesn’t seem like very long. After all, time doesn’t necessarily only fly when you’re having fun. Modern life and its many attendant worries, demands, and distractions tends to speed our clocks and calendars along. This is not usually so in the BVI’s , as sublime and relaxing a string of islands as you’ll find anywhere along your travels. Here, time tends to the play the long game for visitors and locals alike. In the 30 days immediately following the passage of Hurricane Irma, though, things were a bit different. The rugged slog toward recovery made the month seem especially long for BVI friends I’ve been in touch with, each day attaching new challenges to what once were the simplest of daily tasks. At the same time, nature was in a hurry; her restoration unencumbered. Everywhere across the islands, endless trees made bare of their leaves quickly returned to green, while brilliant white sands along shores like these at The Baths in Virgin Gorda re-assumed their normal position at the water’s edge after being displaced by Irma’s mighty winds. The BVI’s today –– coming back strong and just as beautiful as ever. *Photo credit: UC fan and Hurricane Irma survivor, Steve Simonsen . Last updated by Steve Bennett on 11/02/2017 . item.description: 🇻🇮 St. Croix Sea Terrace Restaurant Bar at Grapetree Bay Hotel, St. Croix Steve This should be great. By all accounts, it was…back in the day. I’m talking the 1960s and 70s. That’s when the former Grapetree Bay Hotel on my home island of Saint Croix was really humming. The bar pictured here, now part of what’s known as the Sea Terrace Restaurant, was the epicenter of the fun. Developed with Love Grapetree was originally developed by two men, one whose name you may recognize. That would be Fairleigh Dickinson, Jr. His dad, Fairleigh S. Dickinson, Sr., co-founded the university that bears both their names . (The other guy was named Bob Lodge. More on him another time.) The Dickinson’s loved St. Croix. So much so, in fact, that they donated more than 100 acres of land to the U.S. Virgin Islands Government back in 1970. Their intention: to safeguard the area so that it could be used by the people of the Virgin Islands for recreation. In 1978, that land became what’s known today as the Fairleigh Dickinson Territorial Park. (Editor’s note: The donated land includes Cramer Park, the beach my family most frequented in my youth!) Just outside of his namesake Territorial Park sits Fairleigh Dickinson’s Grapetree Bay Hotel. To be here in its earliest days was to revel in one of the Caribbean’s prime leisure travel playgrounds. Grapetree Bay Heyday A diverse array of entertainers performed nightly. Pancho the Singing Fiddler , the V.I.5 Calypso Combo , and The Friendly Instrumentalists are among the many colorfully-cleped acts. Themed dinner nights were special too. Thursday’s Rib and Tenderloin Cookout was a particular standout. So too was the Sunday Crucian Dinner, served and enjoyed in and around the very bar pictured above. Hurricane Hugo , though, ended the good times here in 1989. It wasn’t until 32 years had passed before Grapetree Bay reopened. Even so, though, it’s not like it was. Grapetree Today The Graptree Bay of today is a sleepy place, or at least it was when I happened by in March 2024 to check out the Sea Terrace Restaurant Bar. The same sultry windswept conditions I remembered from visiting here in the 80s remained. Every breath you take at Grapetree Bay is seasoned with sea salt in the most alluring manner possible. Even as the sun beats down, the steady sea breeze keeps you cool. The effect is altogether intoxicating. Sexy. At the same time, though, the new Grapetree Bay is still very much a work in progress. Ruins of the hotel’s villas, felled by Hugo 30+ years ago, continue rotting away just beyond the pool/terrace. The crowds and high times, distant memories. Part of me, though, likes it better this way. The flash and panache of yesteryear was nice, but it was never necessary to have a great time at Grapetree. That breeze and the naturally sweet surrounds were always more than enough. Now, if we can just get the bar to stock a decent rum or two…

item.title: Chenay Bay Beach: Enjoy with Caution?
item.description: 🇻🇮 St. Croix Chenay Bay Beach: Enjoy with Caution? Steve It’s hard to trust much of anything these days. The fake news phenomenon, deep fakes, and various other AI-generated manipulations have us all questioning much of everything. For me, on my most recent trip back home to St Croix , that also included this scene at Chenay Bay Beach. I had just shuffled out of my garden view cottage at Bungalows On The Bay , the hotel formerly known as Chenay Bay. It was the last morning of a five-day/four-night stay. Somehow, though, I hadn’t managed to lay eyes on the beach up that point. If you know me, then you know that’s exceptionally odd, and just because I’m a big time beach-lover either. (Check out our rundown of the very best Caribbean beaches .) You see, during my childhood years in St Croix, Chenay Bay was one of my favorite beaches. Not necessarily for limin’ in the sand catching sun pursuits either. My usual fun here involved getting out in that water and snorkeling the point just off to the right. The rocks and lively corals that used to abound here attracted all types of tropical sea life. You couldn’t dip your head beneath the waves without hearing of scores of parrotfish scraping their teeth against the rocks and corals to extract their algae treats. Eels, turtles, lobsters – they all hung out here. I’m not sure what the snorkeling is like at Chenay Bay Beach these days. (Snapping this pic is as close as I got to the water here on my June 2025 visit.) That caution sign, though, gives me a bit of pause. I mean, just look at this scene… Flat-calm seas. Near-clear skies. Zero sargassum in sight. I don’t know about you, but I don’t get the sense that there’s anything to be overly cautious about here…unless, perhaps, you’re wary of having a good time? Seriously, if you know what this sign is all about, please drop us a line , or let us know in the comments section below.

item.title: Cinnamon Cay, Saint John
item.description: 🇻🇮 St. John Cinnamon Cay, Saint John Steve As uninhabited islets go, Cinnamon Cay, located just offshore Cinnamon Bay Beach in St John, is often fairly crowded. That is to say, its surrounding seas regularly attract scores of people. Fun-loving, adventure-seeking people. Undersea environs here, you see, are among the most popular spots for snorkel and scuba diving fun in Saint John. At the same time, the generally calm-clear conditions here also make Cinnamon Cay pretty great for kayaking and paddle boarding . An on-site water sports concession rents everything you might need to enjoy the beach and its namesake islet. So, what might you see if you decide to take the plunge and do a little snorkeling here? Well, as elsewhere across the tropics around the world, the coral here isn’t as vibrant and alive as it used to be. The collection of fish and other sea creatures, though, remains fairly abundant. Blue tang, parrotfish, silver sides, barracuda, snapper, stingrays, and turtles all abound here. Personally, I always seem to run across a nurse shark when snorkeling between the beach and the Cay. They’re harmless, of course. Just don’t provoke them, or anything else you might come across exploring these waters.

item.title: Pelican Island BVI Casts A Spell Worthy Of Its Old Name
item.description: 🇻🇬 British Virgin Islands Pelican Island BVI Casts A Spell Worthy Of Its Old Name Steve Pelican Island BVI is as pretty as any corner of the Caribbean . Imagine mooring here and plunging into those sweetly cerulean seas? Imagine chilling on that brilliant white sand beach! Looks like heaven, right? Really makes you wonder how the islet came to be known by its previous name: Witch Island . I mean, there’s nothing spooky, dark, or scary about this place. Maybe the name was meant to keep people away. If I was lucky enough to have found Pelican Island unnamed, I certainly wouldn’t be in a hurry to share it with anyone else. Or maybe the old name purposely played up the paradise. After all, Pelican Island BVI definitely casts a sweet spell on all who happen along here, be it by boat or broomstick . *Photo credit: Patrick Bennett
